examples.problem_statement: Plot a graph of stress (vertically) against strain (horizontally). Find (a) Young’s modulus of elasticity for aluminium, which is given by the gradient of the graph, (b) the value of the strain at a stress of 20N/mm² and (c) the value of the stress when the strain is 0.00020

solution.description: Start by plotting the tabulated stress values up the vertical axis against strain along the horizontal axis. For a material obeying Hooke's law the points should fall on a straight line through the origin, and that drawn line is what all three parts of the question are read from.

Young's modulus is the gradient of that line, so divide a stress reading by the strain that produced it. Taking the point where the strain is 0.0002 and the stress is 14 N/mm squared gives 14 divided by 0.0002, that is 70000 N/mm squared.

Restate the modulus in SI units. One square millimetre is 10 to the power minus 6 square metres, so 1 N/mm squared equals 10 to the power 6 pascals, and 70000 N/mm squared becomes 70 times 10 to the power 9 Pa.

Part (b) reverses the gradient calculation: with the modulus known, strain is stress divided by E. Dividing 20 by 70000 gives 0.000286 to three significant figures, and the 0.000285 read straight off the graph is equally acceptable at this precision.

Part (c) uses the same relation the other way round, multiplying the modulus by the given strain. E times 0.00020 is 70000 times 0.00020, which is 14 N/mm squared, the very point used to fix the gradient in step 2.

examples.problem_statement: Problem 15: Plot R (ohms) vs V (volts), find gradient, intercept, equation, and specific values.

solution.operation: Plot points (16,30), (29,48.5), etc., and draw best straight line through them.
solution.description: Mark each measured pair, such as (16, 30) and (29, 48.5), on axes with V horizontal and R vertical, then rule the single straight line that passes as evenly as possible among them. Experimental points rarely sit exactly on a line, so it is this best straight line, not the raw points, that the gradient is taken from.

Pick two widely spaced points on that drawn line and divide the rise AB by the run BC. The rise from 10 to 135 is 125 and the run from 0 to 100 is 100, so the gradient is 125 divided by 100, which is 1.25 ohms per volt.

examples.problem_statement: Experimental values of $x$ and $y$, shown below, are believed to be related by the law $y = ax^2 + b$. By plotting a suitable graph, verify this law and determine approximate values of $a$ and $b$

solution.operation: Identify the given law and required transformation
solution.description: Read the proposed law y = a x squared + b and notice it is not linear in x, so a plot of y against x would be a curve from which no gradient could be read. The way in is to treat the whole of x squared as one variable.

solution.operation: Transform the equation to linear form
solution.description: Put X in place of x squared. The law then reads y = aX + b, which is the equation of a straight line, with a playing the part of the gradient and b the part of the vertical intercept.

Square every tabulated x value and plot y up the vertical axis against X, that is x squared, along the horizontal axis. If the proposed law really governs the data these transformed points lie close to one straight line, and that straightness is the verification the question asks for.

Take two well separated points on the drawn line and divide the change in y by the change in X, that is by the difference of the squared x values, not of the x values. This gradient is the value of a in the original law.

Finish with b, the value of y where the line meets the vertical axis at X equal to zero. If the plotted range never reaches X equal to zero, take any point on the line instead and compute b as y minus a times X.

examples.answer: The law $y = a x^2 + b$ is verified by plotting $y$ against $x^2$. The gradient $a$ and y-intercept $b$ can be determined approximately from the resulting straight line graph.

key_reminders: {'point': "The text uses bolding for the key term 'determination of law'."}
common_mistakes: Plotting y against x instead of against x squared, which leaves a curve and makes any gradient read from it meaningless.
Computing the gradient as the change in y over the change in x rather than over the change in x squared.
Reading the intercept b at the left-hand edge of the plotted range instead of where the horizontal coordinate x squared is zero.

examples.problem_statement: Solve the equation 2x^3 - 7x^2 + 4x + 4 = 0 graphically.

solution.result: \text{Using Rational Root Theorem: } \pm\frac{\text{factors of constant term}}{\text{factors of leading coefficient}} = \pm\frac{1,2,4}{1,2}
solution.description: Before drawing anything, look for exact roots. The Rational Root Theorem restricts any rational root to a factor of the constant term 4 divided by a factor of the leading coefficient 2, so only a short list of candidates has to be tested.
Write that list out in full. The factors of 4 are 1, 2 and 4 and the factors of 2 are 1 and 2, giving the candidates plus or minus 1, 2, 4 and one half.

Test the candidate x = 2 by synthetic division against the coefficients 2, -7, 4, 4. The last entry of the bottom row is 0, so the remainder vanishes and 2 is confirmed as a root; the other entries of that row are the quotient 2x squared - 3x - 2.
The cubic has now been reduced to a quadratic, which factorises directly: 2x squared - 3x - 2 splits into (2x + 1)(x - 2).
Reassemble the whole cubic from the factor x - 2 found by the division and the two factors just obtained, giving (x - 2)(2x + 1)(x - 2). Notice that x - 2 has now appeared twice.
Set each factor to zero in turn. The factor x - 2 gives x = 2 and the factor 2x + 1 gives x = minus one half. Because x - 2 occurs twice, x = 2 is a double root rather than two separate solutions.

solution.result: \text{Graph of } y = 2x^3 - 7x^2 + 4x + 4 \text{ crosses x-axis at } x = -0.5 \text{ and touches at } x = 2
solution.description: Finally check the algebra against the graph the question asked for. The curve y = 2x cubed - 7x squared + 4x + 4 cuts the horizontal axis at x = -0.5 but only touches it at x = 2, which is exactly how a repeated root shows itself graphically.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Remember: Graphical solutions require accurate plotting and reading of intercepts to desired precision.'}
{'point': 'Caution: When a graph touches but does not cross the x-axis, it indicates a repeated root.'}
{'point': 'Tip: Use symmetry or known factorizations to verify graphical results.'}
{'point': 'Difficulty: Problems 1–2 require plotting; Problems 3–6 require graphical estimation; Problem 7 requires algebraic insight beyond graphing.'}
common_mistakes: Stopping once x = 2 has been found and missing that the factor x - 2 appears twice, so x = 2 is a double root.
Solving 2x + 1 = 0 as x = one half instead of minus one half.
Assuming the curve must cross the horizontal axis at every root, when at x = 2 it only touches it.
